WITH THE PRINCIPAL PATHOGENETIC EFFECTS OF THE MEDICINES ON THE MOST IMPORTANT ORGANS AND FUNCTIONS OF THE BODY
COMPILED FROM THE BEST Hai3BO20PATHIC AUTHORITIES, 1Y
1851. Entered according to Act of Congress; in the year 1851,

The design in the compilation of this Manual has been threefold : first — to furnish Physicians, and especially beginners in Homoeopathic practice, with a convenient Vade Mecum, or work of ready reference, at the bedside of the patient. Secondly : to provide Travellers, who are liable to attacks of illness where it is impossible to procure the servicesof a Homoeopathic physician, with a valuable Medical Companion. And lastly, to supply Families^ residing at a distance from any Homoeopathic physician, with a work which may be used by them, as a Family Physician in cases of emergency, and for many of the minor ills that flesh is heir to. Yet in reference to the use of this work in families, and by laymen in general, the compiler would remark, that no individuals whose knowledge of Medicine, or acquaintance with Homoeopathy, is limited to this, or any similar production, should assume the responsibility of treating severe and dangerous diseases, except in cases of emergency, and then, only until the services of a Homoeopathic physician can be procured; for neither this Manual, nor any work of the kind ever published, can supply the place of the intelligent Homoeopathic physician at the bedside of the patient. In the compilation of this Manual, the Materia Medica of Hahnemann, the Manuals of Jahr and Bonninghausen, the Transactions of the American Institute of Homoeopathy, the works of Hartman, Hering, Laurie, and other distinguished Homoeopathic writers and practitioners have been consulted the for the most of diseases have been given the effects of the Medicines, on the most important Organs, and Functions of the Body, with their relative value typographically distinguished under their respective heads ; and Alphabetically and Nosologically arranged in the following order, viz : The most important Diseases, Organs, and Functions of the body — General Symptoms and Sensations — Causes and Characteristics of diseases, and such Affections as have a Pathological name, are given as Primary Heads, and printed in CAPITALS. Under these Primary heads, are given, in Small Capitals, the Symptoms, Causes, Conditions, Concomitants, Varieties of the Disease, etc., belonging to each primary head. Under these Subordinate heads, which are printed! in Small Capitals, are given, in Italics, the variety of Symptoms, Sensations, Causes, Conditions, etc., belonging to each subordinate head ; and thus the print, following in the descending order, distinguishes the Subordinate from the Primary heads. A glance at the Manual will show its arrangement, and by bearing in mind its Alphabetical order > it will be easily understood.

The Medicines have been divided into three classes, according to their relative value, as indicated by the print. Those printed in Capitals, are medicines, which, from their pathogenetic, or curative effects, are most frequently indicated for the diseases, symptoms, sensations, etc., under the head of which they appear. Those printed in Italics, are medicines of high relative value, but less frequently indicated than those printed in Capitals. The medicines printed in simple Roman letters, are those which in general, are the least frequently indicated, and possess the lowest relative value.

Yet too much importance must not be attached to the relative value of the medicines as indicated by the print, as in many cases the Pathogenetic effects of those medicines which are set down as being of the lowest relative value, will be found bearing the nearest resemblance to the Symptoms manifested by the disease, and in all such cases, they are medicines of the highest relative value, and are to be selected in preference to those printed in capitals, or italics.

The fundamental principle of Homoeopathic practice — the law op cure — as discovered, demonstrated, and promulgated by the illustrious Hahnemann, and expressed by the maxim " Similia Similibus Curantur," is, that ** diseases are cured most

5 quickly, safely, and effectually, by medicines which are capable of producing symptoms SIMILAR to those existing in the patient, and which characterize his disease :" for in accordance with the therapeutic law of similarity, medicines cure affections Similar, or like unto those they produce. Laymen, in the selection of a remedy, should, in the first place, carefully note down all the Symptoms of which the patient complains, together with the state of mind, and characteristics of the disease, as regards its aggravation or amelioration according to time, circumstances, etc. then proceed to collect from under the heads of the various organs functions sensations all those medicines the effects of which correspond to tlie various symptoms sensations characteristics of the disease then from the list of medicines thus collected select exhibit that medicine the effects of which most nearly correspond to all the symptoms sensations characteristics of the disease especially to all the most *and of the

If the disease is one which has a given or pathological name, it will be well for laymen, after they have made their selection of a remedy according to the directions above given, to look under the head of such given name of the disease, and see if the remedy selected is there enumerated, or set down, as being one of the remedies usually indicated in the treatment of such disease and if it is there found especiallyif it is there distinguished as being of high relative value it will strengthen the probability that the selection has been judiciously But if the remedy is not found under the head of such given name of the disease a re-examination should be made in order to that no error has been committed in the selection of the Yet if after such re-examination it does not appear that any error has been made in the selection but that the remedy chosen most nearly corresponds to the totality of the symptoms characteristics of the disease it should then be exhibited in preference to any other whether found under the head of the disease

If, in making the selection of a remedy, the choice should fall between two or more remedies which seem equally indicated according to the totality of the symptoms, and characteristics of the disease, the preference should be given to that remedy which is distinguished by the print as being of the highest relative value.

If the producing cause of any given case of disease is discoverable, and is such that its removal falls within the province of medicine, as grief, fright, repelled cutaneous eruptions, etc., especial reference should be had, in connection with the symptoms, to those remedies, under the head of the said disease producing cause.

ON POTENCIES. The medicines have been used by physicians at various Potencies, from the Mother tinctures, to the two thousandth attenuation. It is recommended, that laymen who use this Manual, should make use of potencies ranging from the third, to the thirtieth attenuation and in such cases as require a higher lower attenuation in order to complete the cure the choice selection of the potency should be left to the judgment of an experienced

The medicines may be administered by placing three or four globules of medicated pellets on the tongue, or eight or ten pellets may be dissolved in an ordinary sized tumbler two-thirds full (about a gill and a half) of pure soft water, and agitated or stirred for several minutes, until the medicine is perfectly dissolved and incorporated with the water and a tea-spoonful of the solution given to children and a small dessert table-spoonful to the medicines are used in the form of from one to three drops of the dilution one-third of an ordinary sized penknife blade full (about one grain in weight) of the trituration may be prepared in the same quantity of water administered in the same manner as directed for the pellets in should be taken that the vessel — tumbler cup in which the medicine is prepared should be perfectly clean and a tumbler glass vessel should always be preferred in the preparation of the which have been long used as coffee tea cups are objectionable especially if the glazing is cracked worn off or

The medicine should be kept in a cool place, free from odors of every description, and so closely covered as to prevent the access of air. The spoon, unless it be made of silver, should never be suffered to remain in the medicine the same vessel should never be used for different medicines until it has been washed thoroughly

It is difficult to give explicit directions for tfie repetition of doses, as the time must necessarily vary according to the* nature of the disease and circumstances of the case. Consequently much must depend on the judgment and discrimination of the administrator. In acute diseases, the proper interval between the repetition of doses, will, in general, vary from one to six hours, according to the nature of the case, or severity of the disease. In those severe and dangerous diseases, which rapidfy run their course to a fatal termination, unless arrested in itoeir progress, as Croup, Cholera, etc., it may be necessary at the commencement of the treatment, to repeat the dose at intervals' of every ten* twenty, or thirty minutes, until there be a mitigation of the symptoms, when the interval between the doses should be lengthened as the patient improves. . In chronic diseases, the proper interval between the repetition of doses, will vary from twelve hours to as many or more days. Laymen, in prescribing^ for chronic diseases, should, after the exhibition of the remedy selected, carefully watch the result, and if after the lapse of twelve, or twentyfour hours, no effect of the medicine is discoverable, and the disease remains apparently the same, the same remedy may be repeated at intervals of every twelve, or twenty-four hours and if after several repetitions of the medicine no* effect is discoverable it should be discontinued another remedy selected exhibited the same precaution as If an improvement follows the exhibition of a remedy no more medicine should be given while the improve* ment when it ceases the remaining symptoms still indicate the same remedy it may be If after the exhibition of a remedy a slight aggravation of the symptoms characteristic of the medicine should speedily tollow its administration no more medicine should be given but we should patiently await the If the aggravation has been produced by the medicine it will soon subside and be followed by an improvement in the condition of the patient which improvement should not be interfered but permitted to proceed without any more medicine until there is no further progress toward a cure afterwards the same remedy may be repeated unless some other remedy is more clearly indicated by the remaining

If the medicinal aggravation should be violent, and harass* ing to the patient, it may be necessary to counteract the effects of the medicine by a suitable antidote afterward when the aggravation shall have entirely subsided the same medicine shall still be indicated it may be repeated and a severe aggravation guarded against by administering a much smaller

It is necessary that laymen, and beginners in Homoeopathic practice, should guard against a too frequent change of medicines. It may be laid down as a general rule, that a medicine which has been carefully selected and exhibited in conformity to the directions herein given for the selection and exhibition of remedies, should not be changed until a reasonable length of time has been allowed for its action, or while it continues to exert a salutary influence until a change of symptoms shall clearly decidedly indicate some other frequent changing from one remedy to another is a miserable most mischievous Yet a remedy should always be changed after a reasonable length of time has been allowed for its action and we perceive no effect when the effect is unfavorable respecting this last care must be taken not to mistake a slight salutary medicinal aggravation for an unfavorable A medicinal aggravation may be known by the sudden aggravation of the symptoms after the exhibition of the medicine — especially of those symptoms which are characteristic of the medicine exhibited which aggravation will soon subside and be followed by an improvement in the condition of the An unfavorable effect may be known by the gradual progressive aggravation of the disease without its partaking of the characteristics of the medicine without any amelioration in the sufferings of the patient but rather a continuous increase of suffering the manifestation of such symptoms as belong to the more advanced stages of the All articles of diet, and drinks, which contain medicinal properties, are strictly prohibited under Homoeopathic treatment : as, coffee, green tea, and herb teas of every description ; ginger, pepper, vinegar, mustard, allspice, cinnamon, cloves, and spices of all kinds : and every variety of vegetable food of an aromatic or medicinal character; as onions, garlic, asparagus, radishes, tomatoes, celery, parsley, parsnips. INTRODUCTION; 9 artichokes, mushrooms* etc.; and every variety of animal food, strong scented^ or difficult of digestion ; as old smoked meat, bacon, fat pork, sausages, tongue, veal cutlets, rancid butter, strong cheese, and the flesh of ail very young animals : in short, every variety of food usually considered objections* ble, or of a doubtful character for invalids, is strictly prohibited under Homoeopathic treatment. In acute diseases, the diet 'should consist of the most light and nutritious kinds of food; such as toast water, barley water, rice water, panada, arrowroot gruel, and such other light and simple kinds of food as are generally allowed in such cases. When the more violent symptoms of the disease have subsided, and the patient is convalescent, more substantial food may be allowed, in moderate quantities, such as beef tea, chicken tea, boiled rice, farina, toast, rice and bread puddings, light bread, and biscuits free from soda or pearfash, and not newly baked : and in most cases, where there is neither colic nor diarrhoea, svjeet, ripe, and juicy fruits may be allowed in moderate quantities at a time, such as sweet grapes, sweet cherries, and ripe peaches.

In chronic diseases, almost every variety of wholesome, nutritious, and easily digested food may be allowed, providing it does not answer the description of such kinds of aliments as are above prohibited.

As a drink, pure water should be allowed in all cases,' except it disagree with the patient, and in such cases toast water, barley water, or rice water should be substituted. In addition to what has already been said under the prer ceding heads, it is important, under Homoeopathic treatment, to enjoin the absolute necessity of guarding against all extraneous influences which may have a tendency to neutralize or counteract the effects of the medicines — as medicated baths and poultices, the smelling of camphor, hartshorn, cologne, and all kinds of flowers and perfumery. Cosmetics and tooth powders are to be avoided all kinds of artificial mineral waters distilled fermented liquors unless allowed by the room of the sick should be well ventilated and be kept free from all
Flowers, and plants of every description, should always be excluded from the chamber of the sick. Strong mental

emotions, as anger, grief, care, etc., should be guarded against. In short, every variety of circumstance, whether of a physical or moral nature, which might have a tendency to counteract the influence of the medicines, or retard the recovery of the patient, should be carefully avoided.

CONCLUSION. In presenting this work to the profession and the public, the Compiler would remark, that he has by much labor, diligent research, and careful comparison, endeavored to compile a large amount of valuable matter, in a correct, brief, and comprehensive manner. Yet it is not pretended that this Manual is a full, complete, or perfect Repertory, or that in its compilation all errors have been avoided, and especially such as regard the true value of the remedies in all cases, as indicated by the print. Yet the Compiler flatters himself that the work will be found in the main, as substantially correct as any other of the kind that has vet appeared in the English language and if the work as it is shall be found to answer the general purposes for which it is intended contribute in any degree to the advancement of the interests of the consequent relief of human suffering the object in its compilation will have been J B

AMAUROSIS (gutta serena, paralysis of the optic nerve).

Blindness without obscuration of the humors of the eye. The pupil is dilated, and the contractility and sensibility of the iris to light is greatly diminished, or entirely annihilated. In amaurosis erethistica, the blindness is only partial, and the symptoms nearly the reverse of the above ; the eye exhibiting an extreme sensibility to light, the patient seeing best at dusk, or when the light is very feeble ; all colors appear brighter, and white objects appear brilliant : the pupil is contracted — sometimes movable, and at other times distorted, and sometimes contracting in a very irregular manner. In either form of the disease the cure is often difficult. The principal remedies, are, In General, for Amaurosis Incipient, or complete

Drowning (from) : Elevate the head and shoulders, cleanse the mouth and nostrils, apply friction and heat ; and give Lachesis on the tongue, and in injections. If these means fail, place the body in a warm bath, rub briskly, yet gently with the hand ; cautiously apply spirits of hartshorn, or spirits of camphor to the nostrils, and carefully endeavor to inflate the lungs. It is said that passing a stream of electricity or galvanism through the chest promises to be of great service. Frost or Cold (from) : Rub or cover the body with snow, or use a cold salted bath. ASTHMA (a disease in which difficulty of breathing is the predominant symptom).

Dyspnoea without fever, occurring in paroxysms attended with a sensation of suffocating constriction of the chest, with cough, and wheezing respiration. In some cases the cough is dry {asthma sicca), in other cases the cough is attended with expectoration (asthma pituita) ; the expectoration is at first scanty and glutinous, and afterward more copious ; relief is generally afforded as the expectoration increases in quantity. Pale, sickly complexion, deficient warmth, lassitude, physical and mental weakness, emaciation, depraved appetite, weak digestion, palpitation of the heart, and oedema of the feet and lower extremities, are some of the most prominent symptoms of this disease. Remedies, In General

In the most common variety of this disease, the attacks are usually preceded by a diarrhoea, in which the evacuations, consisting at first of fecal matters, shortly become yellowish, greenish, and watery, and finally flocculent, having the appearance of rice water with little flocks or specks floating in it. Shortly after this, the patient is attacked with violent vomiting, and purging, cramps, pains in the stomach and abdomen, with great anxiety, weakness, coldness of the extremities, or of the whole surface of the body. The urine and perspiration is entirely suppressed ; the pulse small, intermittent, or imperceptible ; the skin cold and bluish, and the countenance hippocratic. In General, the Principal Remedies are In the majority of ordinary cases of Cholera, two drops of the Tincture of Camphor should be given in a dessertspoonful of sugar water, every ten or twenty minutes, during the first hour ; and if improvement follow, continue the remedy at longer intervals, until the most alarming symptoms have subsided, when some other
remedy should be selected in accordance with the remaining symptoms.

and verat. may be given in alternation, once in fifteen minutes at the commencement of the treatment, and the interval between the repetition of doses lengthened as the patient improves. In all cases, where there is neither thirst, vomiting, not purging, but rapid failure of strength, blueness, and icy coldness of the body, burning pains in the stomach, inconsolable anguish, and dread of suffocation, give Camphor, as above directed. If spasms ensue, with cramps in the calves of the legs, great thirst, weakness, excessive coldness, frequent, sudden, and violent vomiting and purging, Veratrum is the principal remedy. If, in addition to vomiting and diarrhoea, there is pressure in the stomach and epigastrium, violent pains in the abdomen, spasmodic colic, and bloody evacuations — Cuprum should be exhibited. When there is great anxiety, excessive anguish, fear of death, violent thirst, intolerable burning in the stomach and bowels, with cutting, cramplike pains in the abdomen, scalding evacuations, cold and clammy skin, Arsenicum is the remedy. In the last stages of Cholera, or Stage of Collapse, give cupr. hydr-ac. laur. phos. ph-ac. sec. or veratrum, in accordance with the particular symptoms, which see : under their respective heads.

A painful gouty inflammation of the hip-joint, frequently terminating in suppuration (coxarthrocace). The pain frequently extends upward to the loins, and downward to the front part of the knee, and is greatly aggravated by motion, and stepping on the affected limb. It is distinguished from sciatica by the pain being ameliorated by rest, and by its not following the course of the sciatic nerve. Remedies, In General : A con. arg. ars. asa. aur.
mang. Merc, nitr-ac. nux-v. puis. rhus. sep. staph, sulph.

Chronic inflammation of the hip-joint ; which, if unchecked, terminates in suppuration and caries, destroying the head of the femur, and producing luxation outward and upward. At the commencement of the disease, the pain is usually felt in the knee, and is sometimes mistaken for a disease of that joint, a mistake that should be carefully guarded against. The pain is aggravated by motion and pressure, and ameliorated by rest (distinguishing it from sciatica). The disease is most frequently met with in children. Remedies, In General

Coma, or constant delirium, or both united ; with fever, and signs of sanguineous congestion to the head. When the inflammation occupies the membranes of the brain (meningitis), pain is present, and is sometimes violent ; when seated m the substance of the brain, it is attended with a sensation of weight or pressure rather than of pain. The inflammation, however, generally includes both the brain and its membranes ; and, in addition to the above-named symptoms, there is usually great heat in the head, violent throbbing of the carotid and temporal arteries, redness and fullness of the face and eyes, the pulse variable — sometimes quick, weak, and intermittent, and sometimes very full, slow, and strong. The pupils of the eyes are often immovable, and in the early stage of the disease contracted ; but as the disease progresses they become dilated, and the eyes void of expression. Grasping at the head, sudden starts, heavy sleep, or constant agitation and tossing about, with great sensibility to noise, fits of screaming (especially in children), and disposition to bury the head in the pillow, are, with various other phenomena, as nausea, vomiting, and involuntary evacuations, concomitant symptoms of inflammation of the brain. A peculiar kind of inflammation, presenting a superficial shining redness of the skin, which disappears on pressure, but returns as soon as the pressure is removed. Severe attacks of this disease are usually ushered in with a chill, succeeded by heat, nausea, headache, and symptoms of gastric derangement, with a greater or less degree of fever. The inflammation is accompanied with pricking, burning, pungent, or scalding pain. In some cases, blisters form on the inflamed surface (erysipelas pustulosum), which sometimes degenerate into very painful and malignant suppurations (erysipelas gangrenous). When the face and head are attacked, it is frequently attended with violent cerebral affections, as sopor, and delirium. Remedies, In General

A constant burning stitching pain in the region of the stomach, increased by inspiration, pressure, or food ; with bloating, tension, and heat in the epigastric region, frequently combined with pulsation. There is great anxiety and restlessness, with sobbing, hiccough, nausea, retching, and vomiting up of whatever is taken into the stomach, even of pure cold water.. There is also violent thirst, small wiry pulse, great prostration, coldness of the extremities, and sometimes fits of fainting, spasms, and convulsions. The tongue is generally dry, foul, and rough in the centre, and red at the tip and around the edges. Remedies, In General

When the inflammation is seated on the outer surface or convex side of the liver, there is severe pain in the right hypochondrium, accompanied with burning, or stitches, which extend to the shoulder and sternum, and sometimes even to the right foot. The pain, and the short dry cough attendant on the disease, is increased by inspiration, and the patient finds it impossible to lie on the right side. When the inflammation occupies the concave part or substance of the liver, the patient complains of a sensation of pressure rather than of pain in the region of the liver, and finds it difficult or impossible to lie on the left side. In this case the biliary system is more affected,, and the countenance sometimes assumes a complete jaundiced appearance, with bitter taste in the mouth, vomiting, and high-colored urine. In either case, the right hypochondrium is bloated, hot, and painful on pressure ; with dry skin, hard quick pulse, thirst, high-colored urine, and the usual signs of inflammatory fever. The usual symptoms of hydrocephalus are, drowsiness, stupidity, squinting, dilated pupils, grinding of the teeth, sudden starts, grasping at the head, fits of screaming, delirium, and sometimes deep sopor. The eyes are usually red, and void of expression, or have a peculiar staring look, with trembling of the pupil. Paroxysms of fever, usually commencing with a chill followed by heat, and terminating in sweat. The paroxysms usually occur every twenty-four hours (quotidian), or forty-eight hours (tertian), or seventy-two hours (quartan), and in some cases at intervals of seven days (octanae). Sometimes the paroxysms occur twice within the above-named periods, and are called double quotidian, tertian, or quartan, &c. The period between the paroxysms is called the apyrexia, during which the patient is usually free from fever and suffering. Remedies, In General

An eruption of pointed vesicles with a reddish margin, attended with an intolerable itching, aggravated by the heat of the bed. On their first appearance they are filled with a limpid fluid, which subsequently degenerates into scabs, either dry, moist, or suppurating. The eruption appears first between the fingers, on the wrists, and bends of the joints, and frequently extends over the whole surface of the body. It is contagious by contact, and its duration is indefinite. Remedies, In General

Acute Laryngitis bears a strong resemblance to Croup, but is distinguished from it by the constant disposition to hawk in order to clear the larynx, rather than the involuntary and violent cough attendant on croup. There is usually present, hoarseness, laborious respiration, extreme sensibility of the larynx to pressure, difficult and painful deglutition, fever, thirst, hard quick pulse, and in some cases spasmodic contraction of the larynx during the act of swallowing, which is sometimes attended with danger of immediate suffocation. This disease is characterized by thick, rough, swollen, disorganized skin, with rose-colored tuberosities, or large white spots, with scaling of the epidermis ; or the skin is covered with crusts or scabs, discharging from intermediate places a thick, fetid, or corrosive ichor. In Lepra Orientalis, which is infectious, the whole surface of the body is covered with crusts, scabs, and corrosive ulcers, with excessive pains, and entire destruction of the whole cutaneous system. An attack of this disease is generally preceded by a stiffness in the back of the neck, and lower jaw sometimes there is difficult deglutition oppressive tightness of the chest impeded respiration previous to the setting in of As the disease advances the muscles become spasmodically contracted the jaws closely firmly set (trismus) body is generally drawn 18

Lock-jaw backward (opisthotonos) ; or, as is sometimes the case, the body is bent forward (emprosthotonos) ; or to one side (pleurosthotonos) ; and finally, the head, trunk and extremities become spasmodically and rigidly extended ; or drawn backward, forward, or on one side, as the case may be, with frightful distortions of the countenance. If the disease is not arrested, the spasms (which do not continue unremittingly,) become more and more severe, and death generally ensues about the fourth day from the commencement of spasms. In Measles, the premonitory symptoms, or stage of irritation, is ushered in by symptoms of a common cold or catarrh ; with sneezing,
short, dry cough, redness and lachrymation of the eyes,

intolerance of light, fever, and sometimes headache. This stage of the disease lasts for three or four days, when an eruption of small red spots, of one or two lines in diameter, make their appearance generally on the face neck arms first finally extend over the whole surface of the second stage of the disease stage of florescence lasts for three four days a greater less degree of intensity of the above-named symptoms when the eruption turns pale disappears a bran-like desquamation of the epidermis in the same order in which it sprang

The last stage, or stage of desquamation, generally commences about the ninth or tenth day of the disease, and lasts for several days. This disease is characterized by critical perspiration, and urine, during the stage of desquamation and in some cases by diarrhoea which is considered a salutary disease may be simple benign complicated malignant Remedies, In General :

An eruption of innumerable, transparent, white, purple, or scarlet vesicular elevations, appearing on all parts of the body, and especially on the chest. The eruption is preceded by fever, sour smelling perspiration, dry cough, anxiety, oppressed respiration, and frequently accompanied with sighing and moaning. The fever, and the preceding symptoms, usually subside after the eruption makes its appearance, but sometimes continue, and even increase in severity, after the eruption has come out. It usually terminates by a slight desquamation of the epidermis. Remedies, In General :

A large, white, and rapidly formed leuco-phlegmatic and very painful swelling of the leg and thigh ; sometimes extending over the whole pelvic region. This disease is analogous to puerperal fever, and has been denominated puerperal fever without the peritoneum. It usually happens within the first fortnight after parturition, and lasts from eight to fourteen days, and terminates by resolution, or the formation of lacteal abscesses, or death by gangrene. rubrics.text: rhus. rata. samb. sil. squill, val. verat. MUCOUS FEVER.

The precursory symptoms of mucous fever (erethism of the mucous membrane of the intestinal canal), are, loss of appetite, flat slimy taste, white slimy coating of the tongue, pressure, fullness, and distension of the stomach, irregular evacuations, pale countenance, and other symptoms similar to the precursors of gastric fever, with which disease it is liable to be confounded, but is distinguished from it by the peculiar slimy coating of the tongue, and the characteristic secretion of mucus. As the disease progresses, the white mucous coating of the tongue becomes dark red at the tip and edges, indicative of a typhoid condition, although it sometimes remains white through the whole course of the disease. The patient frequently ejects from the stomach a white tasteless mucus, and the introduction of the least quantity of food is followed by tension, pressure, and distension of the stomach. The evacuations from the bowels consist principally of a tenacious, albuminous and thready mucus, mixed with undigested food, the coloring matter of bile, and pieces of worms. The pulse is usually soft, and seldom accelerated ; the thirst moderate, although in some cases the patient has a great desire for drink. The urine is straw-colored, loamy, or flocculent, and deposits a whitish sediment. The skin is usually moist and warm, and the patient restless, peevish, languid, and weak. Remedies, In General

rubrics.text: Pain in some part or spot in the spinal column, which
may be permanent, or returning at indefinite periods.
The pain, which is aggravated by motion, and increased
by pressure, is usually slight when the patient is at
rest, and in some cases entirely wanting. The inflammation may be acute, or chronic, and in the latter case

232 NAILS. Myelitis it is sometimes difficult of recognition. It is generally associated with or productive of paralysis, usually of the lower extremities ; yet sometimes of the upper, and in some cases affecting the internal organs. If the inflammation is situated in the cervical vertebrae, it frequent]^ produces aphonia, dysphagia, and spasms of the pharynx and neck; if in the upper dorsal vertebrae, anxiety, oppressed respiration, palpitation of the heart, and sometimes opisthotonos ; if the lower dorsal or lumbar vertebrae be the seat of the inflammation, it is frequently productive of paralytic or spasmodic affections of the abdomen or pelvic viscera. The seat of the disease may be detected by pressing on each single vertebra of the whole spinal column, or by passing a sponge wet with warm water along the spine, the affected part being sensitive to the pressure, or to the touch of the warm sponge. PEMPHIGUS (vesicular eruption, with or without fever).

An eruption of vesicles, varying in size from a split pea to a walnut, rilled with a serous fluid, and resembling blisters arising from a scald. The disease may be attended with fever (acute pemphigus), which generally lasts for several days, when the vesicles, having arrived at maturity, burst, and form into scabs, of a whitish or light brown color, or pass into painful and protracted ulcerations. The disease, when unaccompanied by fever. (chronic pemphigus), may continue for months, or years, in which case new vesicles continue to form successively as the older ones disappear. This disease is usually ushered in by a chill, followed by heat, fever, oppressed, short, hurried, and painful respiration : with a short, dry, and continuous cough, at the commencement, excited by deep inspiration, or by speaking. The cough is afterwards followed by expectoration of viscous, lumpy, and tenacious mucus, generally of a brownish or brick-dust color ; in some cases, however, pure blood is expectorated, indicating a very high degree of inflammation. In this form of inflammation of the chest, both pain and oppression are present, the pain being more or less severe and of a stitching character, as the pleura or surface of the lungs is more or less the seat of inflammation. Heat, thirst, high-colored urine, hard, quick, wiry pulse, and other symptoms of inflammatory action are always present. Remedies, In General :

Purple, brownish, reddish, or blackish spots in the skin, appearing on all parts of the body, without order or definite periods. They are generally round, and of one or two lines in diameter, yet sometimes irregularly shaped, and appear in large spots of one or two inches in circumference. They may be accompanied with fever (acute petechise or spot-fever), or without fever (chronic petechia) ; or they may appear as a symptom in gastric, verminous, and malignant fevers. In the early stage of the disease, the most prominent symptoms of pulmonary phthisis are, dry cough, oppressed respiration, shortness of breath, emaciation, greatly accelerated pulse, hectic fever, and burning in the palms of the hands and soles of the feet. As the disease advances, night-sweats supervene, the cough becomes more harassing, with expectoration of mucus, or pus, with increased emaciation, and prostration of strength. In the later stages of the disease, the bowels (which in the early stage of the disease are usually costive) generally become relaxed, and severe attacks of diarrhoea ensue, which, with cedematous swelling of the feet and lower extremities, are harbingers of approaching dissolution. When it is ascertained that poisonous substances have been taken into the stomach, we should immediately endeavor to cause their ejection by vomiting, or neutralize their effects by antidotes. Vomiting should be excited by drinking large quantities of tepid water, putting the finger down the throat, or by tickling the

265 Poisons throat with a feather or by placing snuff mustard mixed salt upon the tongue or by mixing a teaspoonful of powdered mustard two teaspoonsful of salt in a tumbler of water let the patient drink it at a draught follow its administration by copious draughts of tepid If these means fail cannot be made use of give injections of tobacco The Principal Antidotes, most safely administered, where the kind of poison is unknown, are : sugar and water ; or white of eggs — especially if there be violent pains in the stomach and bowels ; or strong coffee, if the patient be dull, stupid, giddy, delirious, or raving ; or soap-water in large quantities, where there is reason to suppose the poison to consist of mineral or corrosive acids, and the patient complains of a sour, burning, acrid taste, or acrid scalding heat in the mouth, throat, and stomach, with acute pains in the stomach and bowels.

The characteristics of this disease, are, flaccidity of the muscles, with weakness of the limbs, and enlargement of the epiphysis of the bones, and especially those of the wrists. As the disease progresses, the limbs, spine, sternum, ribs, and pelvis become distorted; and finally a slow fever supervenes, and cough, oppressed respiration, and marasmus ensue. The disease generally manifests itself in children of from one to two years of age, and especially in such as are distinguished by great development of the head and precocity of the mental faculties. RENAL CALCULUS (stone in the kidneys, nephritic calculi).

Renal calculus is productive of permanent or periodic pains, and pressure, in the region of the kidneys, with more or less disturbance of the urinary secretion, and severe attacks of colic and vomiting. Nephritic colic is distinguished by the violence and sudden occurrence of the pains in the region of the kidneys or bladder, spreading over the whole abdomen, and accompanied by vomiting and crying, and affecting sympathetically the testicle and leg of the side diseased. In addition to the above-named symptoms, it is sometimes productive of severe spasms, and especially after the stone has been dislodged, and during its passage through the ureters, when the pains are often of a most excruciating character. RHEUMATISM (inflammation of the fibrous tissue of the body, either acute or chronic).

Pains in the fibrous, muscular, or membranous parts of the body, generally attended with rigidity of the part affected, and aggravation of the pains on motion ; and characterized by sensibility to the changes of the weather, and atmospheric influence. It may appear with fever (acute rheumatism), or without fever (chronic rheumatism) ; it may be local, or wandering from one part of the body to another ; accompanied with swelling, heat, and redness of the skin — or without swelling, heat, or discoloration of the skin ; sometimes the pains are relieved by hot, and sometimes by cold applications, and vice versa. The pains are usually worse during the night, but sometimes worse during the day. In some cases the pains are relieved by motion, and in others by rest. In short, it is a disease which presents such a vanity of phases, and contrariety of symptoms, as makes it difficult to give any definite diagnosis ; yet the disease is one so frequently occurring, and so well known, as to render any particular description unnecessary. SCALD HEAD (tinea capitis, crusta lactea, ringworm of the scalp).

Eruption of little pustules in the hairy parts of the head, sometimes appearing in circular patches, and attended with violent itching and the secretion of a viscous, fetid matter, which forms into scabs. The eruption usually becomes confluent, and the patches uniting with each other, form into thick, hard, and extensive incrustations. The disease is communicable through the use of the same bomb, brush, or towel used by the patient ; and the contagion should be carefully guarded against among children. Remedies, In General

305 Small-pox transparent fluid ; the pustules stand suppurating for three days more, during which time the lymph in the pustules becomes converted into pus, which commences to dry up and form into scabs on the seventh day of the eruption, and the eleventh of the disease. The eruptive stage of the disease lasts three days, during which time new pustules continue to break out ; and as each pustule or pock runs through its regular course, observing the same order and measure of time, the general desiccation does not occur until the fourteenth day of the disease. The pustules make their appearance first on the face and scalp ; the next day on the hands, arms, and neck ; and the third day on the feet and other parts of the body. The pustules sometimes run into each other (confluent small-pox), and form large continuous suppurating surfaces. Remedies, In General

In the treatment of this disease, cool fresh air, cool drinks, and cleanliness, are valuable auxiliaries. As soon as the eruption appears, the room of the patient should be kept dark, in order to prevent the disfiguration of parts exposed to the light. Vaccinin enjoys the reputation of being eminently useful in the treatment of small-pox ; and is said to possess the property of " altering the character of the pustules, so that the usual pits or scarred depressions are completely obviated." Slight chills followed by heat, lassitude, giddiness, and in some cases trembling and fits of fainting, are the usual precursors of typhus fever. The head and nervous system seem particularly affected hence drowsiness stupor delirium are frequently present and in some cases spasms convulsions pulse is often very changeable — sometimes full slow but usually quick soft small pulse does not harmonize the respiration as in inflammatory tongue is usually thickly coated the mouth parched dry but little skin is usually hot dry 6*

320 Typhus Fever but in some cases, the parched and burning skin is succeeded by profuse, clammy, and debilitating perspiration. The urine is sometimes red, and sometimes pale, or brown, or bloody, or turbid, or cloudy, and sometimes deposits a copious sediment. In short, changeability and discordance of symptoms, with slow fever, nervous affections, and great prostration, are the predominant characteristics of Typhus Fever ; the symptoms varying according to the virulence or the variety of the disease, or as the cerebral, abdominal, or pulmonary symptoms predominate. The attack is usually preceded by great lassitude, headache, giddiness, and faintness which is soon succeeded by chilliness great anxiety followed by excessive thirst violent vomiting purging first of bilious then of blackish fetid urine is offensive scanty breathing hurried laborious sometimes attended a gasping for air or deep sighing respiration tongue is usually coated white at the commencement of the attack and is sometimes moist but more frequently dry and as the disease advances it becomes parched red or brownish and in the latter stages of the disease black skin eyes are of a yellow tinge — the restlessness anxiety excessive — the eyes glassy hollow — the head confused frequently there is violent

The pulse is subject to great variations sometimes it is full strong sometimes small weak irregular intermittent As the disease advances unchecked the symptoms become more violent — the vomiting purg-

Yellow Fever ing incessant — the prostration excessive — the features contracted — the pulse sinks — the evacuations become black, or bloody — purple spots make their appearance — and death closes the scene.
